title: Trump bought and sold shares in Musk’s SpaceX in July, financial disclosure shows
summary: Donald Trump bought up to $50,000 worth and sold up to $15,000 of shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX in July,his latest stock buy involving a government contractor.
story: US President Donald Trump bought as much as $50,000 worth of shares and sold as much as $15,000 in Elon Musk’s SpaceX in July, according to a public financial disclosure, his latest transactions involving a government contractor run by his former adviser.

Trump bought between $15,001 and $50,000 worth of shares in SpaceX on July 10, according to a financial disclosure he signed on September 8. He sold between $1,001 and $15,000 worth of shares on July 17, according to the same disclosure.
The latest trades add a new financial link between the president and Musk’s rocket ​company at a time when the administration is making decisions that could affect the firm’s fortunes.
SpaceX priced ​the biggest-ever US IPO on June 12, valuing the space, satellite and ⁠AI provider at $1.77 trillion. Reuters previously reported that Trump bought shares in SpaceX in June.

In a statement to Reuters at the time, White House spokesman Davis Ingle said ​third-party financial institutions independently manage the president’s portfolio and replicate “recognized indexes, such as the Schwab ​1000.”
Trump’s spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the July trades.

The purchase and sale were among more than 1,000 trades the president made in July. The Office of Government Ethics, the team responsible for collecting ethics disclosures from US officials, posted the form on its website on Tuesday.
Reuters could not ​immediately determine the precise amount of Trump’s investment because federal officials use ranges to declare the value of their ​assets on their financial disclosure forms.
SpaceX is ‌a ⁠US military contractor, and often seeks approvals from federal agencies.

title: Trump’s focus on the press distracts Republicans from pocketbook issues
summary: The media ban has dominated the news cycle for days, and rather than steer the conversation back to economic issues, has Trump amplified the furor.
story: WASHINGTON — Zigzagging from issue to issue, President Donald Trump has left his political allies struggling to keep pace with his pronouncements and lost precious time to drive a compelling message ahead of the midterm congressional elections, Republican strategists and people who’ve worked with him said.

The takeaway from recent polling is that voters worry most about high prices and the cost of living. But Trump has at times veered off pocketbook issues and made moves that are peripheral to the top-of-mind concerns of voters who will soon decide which party controls Congress.
The latest instance of Trump stepping on his party’s own messaging came on Friday.

In the hour before he held an Oval Office event focused on reducing prescription drug prices, Trump announced he was barring three news outlets from the White House grounds because he disliked their coverage. That caught even some members of his own staff off guard.
The media ban has dominated the news cycle for days, and rather than steer the conversation back to the savings Americans would reap from his policies, Trump amplified the furor.
Some Republican candidates in competitive races are increasingly distancing themselves from the president, believing that voters want a different focus and tack than what Trump is offering.

Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., who is typically a staunch Trump defender, released an ad criticizing Trump’s mass deportation agenda. And GOP candidates in Iowa and Michigan have spoken out against the Iran war and its effect on prices.

Nearly two-thirds of adults lack confidence in the national news media, according to an NBC News survey in June sponsored by More Perfect, a nonpartisan nonprofit dedicated to advancing democracy. That makes the press a ripe target, though it isn’t clear that Americans want Trump to do something about it.

In an NBC News poll this month, registered voters cited inflation, government corruption, threats to democracy, jobs and the economy, the Iran war, immigration and healthcare costs as issues that loom largest; news coverage was not presented as an option.

“The president is out there touting his new arch,” Maura Gillespie, a Republican strategist, said of Trump’s plan to build a soaring arch near Arlington National Cemetery. “None of that addresses the gas prices being over $4. None of that addresses the younger voters who are struggling to afford their first home. None of that is landing.”
“Republicans need to steer their messaging away from Trump and divert their lane from him and focus on their constituents, because that’s the only thing that’s going to get them elected,” she added.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Trump often complains that news coverage fails to credit him for his successes. Labor and stock markets have proved resilient in Trump’s term, though wages are lagging inflation.

“The story no one is writing is how well the economy is doing in spite of the president’s lack of discipline,” said a person close to the administration, who added that Trump, 80, is growing “more impulsive with age.”
Speaking at the United Nations on Tuesday, Trump spooled out a list of accomplishments on his watch. He struck a triumphal tone as he cast the U.S. as a nation in the midst of a renaissance.

“Our economy is the envy of the world,” he said. “Our military is the most powerful on earth. Our technology is second to none and we’re leading in virtually everything. Our energy is fueling the planet. America is rising, our nation is growing, our power is expanding, our country is doing better than ever before.”

A White House spokesman, Kush Desai, said in a statement: “The Trump administration has remained laser-focused delivering on the president’s long-term economic agenda on the home front. Continued private-sector job growth, booming investments, and month-over-month prices of beef, chicken, prescription drugs, and other essentials declining in the last two inflation reports are all proof that America’s positive economic momentum continues.”
In recent months, Trump has slalomed back and forth through the issues.

In April, he threatened to destroy Iran’s civilization. Hours later, he backed off. He called Iran’s leaders “very rational” in June, “scum” in July. In his United Nations speech, Trump revived his apocalyptic threat. He warned that he may need to “annihilate” Iran and “drive them into hell” if the regime doesn’t agree to a deal to end the war.

This month he announced that he would send every American a $5,000 check if Republicans win the midterm elections; a key Republican senator whose committee oversees spending plans told reporters he had seen no details of how Trump’s idea would work.
“He’s very unpredictable. He calls it trusting his gut,” a second Republican senator told NBC News, who, like others in this piece, requested anonymity to speak candidly.
The press ban
The latest thunderclap from Trump’s social media feed was his eviction of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds.

A number of high-level White House aides were unaware beforehand that Trump had imposed the ban, and they struggled to explain it in the hours after it went into effect, according to conversations with four White House officials. Trump’s chief of staff Susie Wiles was absent from the building Friday when he announced the new directive, according to a person familiar with the situation, potentially leading to some of the confusion from the staff.
Still, aides sought to defend Trump’s move.
“Nobody close to the president was surprised at his action to hold the fake news accountable,” a senior White House official said.

Even Vice President JD Vance seemed at a loss as to how to explain the policy. Trump said specifically that he was “banning” the three outlets. But Vance, speaking to reporters Monday before heading to a campaign stop in North Carolina, said: “So, he’s not banning media outlets. What he’s doing is saying, ‘We’re not going to give you special access to the White House if you engage in what is effectively propaganda.’”
Rubio defends White House media outlet ban

In an interview with the “TODAY” show, Secretary of State Marco Rubio was asked whether media outlets should be banned because Trump doesn’t like their coverage. Rubio defended the president’s decision, saying, “There aren’t a bunch of police officers or soldiers kicking down the doors of MSNBC or MS NOW, whatever it’s called, and arresting people and unplugging it from the grid. They’re just not allowed to work from the workspace at the White House.”
MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner, CNN’s Betsy Klein and Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett were all denied access to the White House on Saturday.
Klein and Haslett both had their White House press credentials confiscated when they sought to enter the grounds.

In his remarks Friday, Trump said, “We are banning them, yes we are, and there may be others to follow.” But a Trump adviser told NBC News on Tuesday “there are not” conversations happening inside the White House about expanding the ban to other disfavored outlets.

The TV networks have set up what’s known as a “pool”; they take turns covering the president as he goes about his public activities and sharing footage with other news outlets. CNN was supposed to provide TV pool coverage on Monday, but the White House barred them from their duties.
In response, the four other networks that are part of the TV network pool — NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox — refused to step in for the exiled CNN, meaning there was no TV pool coverage.

The repercussions were soon evident, potentially impeding Trump’s ability to deliver his message. Newsmax, a conservative outlet, tried to air the president’s remarks at a ribbon-cutting ceremony, but he couldn’t be heard.

“There’s no microphone because the pool cameras aren’t there. So maybe, Tim, this is one example of it backfiring just a little bit,” the Newsmax host said, adding, “So obviously, the ramifications are here. Can’t hear what the president is saying.”

Trump’s ban is now before a judge. All three outlets filed suit against Trump on Monday, arguing that their eviction violates both due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, set a hearing for Wednesday afternoon on the plaintiff’s motion for a temporary restraining order.

Trump has long lamented his media coverage. During his first term, the White House barred a CNN reporter, Jim Acosta, from the grounds following a contentious public exchange with Trump. CNN sued and the judge in the case — also Kelly — ordered the Trump administration to return Acosta’s press pass. In the end, the administration relented and restored the pass permanently.
In the new term, Trump has also talked privately about barring individual reporters and news outlets from the White House, but he refrained, according to two people familiar with those discussions.

By acting now, he may be distracting from a promising message for his party ahead of the midterms. Internal White House polling shows that Trump’s effort to reduce the cost of prescription drugs is his most popular issue, according to a White House official.

“He can and should be talking about the things that voters say are really important to them. And this [the media ban] is not it,” said Douglas Heye, a former communications director for the Republican National Committee. “It seems to have come out of nowhere and it seems to have caught a lot of people by surprise.”

“We’re less than 45 days out from the election and for the last three days no voter has heard anything about what Donald Trump wants to do to lower prices,” he added. “That’s a problem for any Republican on the ballot.”
The second Republican senator rattled off a series of issues that he’d like to see Trump spotlight.
“He can go out and talk about the reduction in crime,” the senator said, “or controlling the border, or eliminating rules and regulations.”
“But he’s probably not.”
‘Be quiet’

A recent run of setbacks has soured the mood inside the West Wing, a senior White House official said. Even though Trump now has a handpicked chairman of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, the board defied Trump’s wishes last week and raised interest rates.
The Supreme Court has blocked Trump’s attempt to use the Postal Service to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the midterms, something Trump had hoped to do.
Gas prices have spiked since the Trump administration and Israel launched the war against Iran on Feb. 28, creating a slow-rolling backlash within the GOP.
Growing numbers of Republicans in tight midterm races are finding ways to distance themselves from Trump, whose approval rating in a new NBC News poll stood at 41%, a second-term low.

Rep. Ashley Hinson, an Iowa Republican who faces a tough race for the Senate, called for an “immediate end” to the Iran war in a social media post Monday. That’s an about-face from Hinson, who has voted against resolutions directing Trump to stop the war six different times.

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Hinson wrote. “We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices.”

On Friday, Trump got some unsolicited advice from an iconic figure in the cultural world. Pat Boone, the 92-year-old singer-songwriter, released a video on X that offered a heartfelt suggestion to the president.

“Right now, I feel like you’re very tired,” Boone said, looking straight at the camera. “And I’m worried that many of us haven’t prayed enough for you because I think you’re wearing out and you’re feeling the pressure and expressing yourself in ways that are not becoming to you — that are not presidential.”
“So may I recommend something very highly: that you be quiet.”

title: Supreme Court declines to intervene in custody case involving newborn with heart condition
summary: The Supreme Court declined to get involved in the case of a surrogate enmeshed in a multistate custody battle with California parents who at one point asked her to abort the fetus because of a heart defect.
story: Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday rejected a request for the Supreme Court to get involved in the case of a surrogate enmeshed in a multistate custody battle with California parents who at one point asked her to abort the fetus because of a heart defect.

McKenna West gave birth to the couple’s baby in Texas last month and argued in court there that California denied her due process when it awarded custody of the child, whom she named Gabriel, to his genetic parents.
A Texas judge dismissed her claims. She then appealed to the Supreme Court. Kagan denied to issue a stay in the case in a Tuesday order with no written decision.

In a filing earlier this month, attorneys for West urged Kagan, who handles emergency matters involving California, to intervene because a “life hangs in the balance.” They said West is concerned that Gabriel might not get the medical care he needs if he remains in the custody of his parents, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar.

Gilkar told a judge in Dallas last month that she and her husband were dedicated to getting the son they named Rumi the help he requires — and that the “unstable” West is making an already tragic situation more fraught.
“She’s making us run from doctor to doctor, state to state with our baby. She’s trying to take him,” Gilkar testified.

The Texas Supreme Court issued a ruling last week allowing the baby to be moved to California, where the parents have medical care for the child lined up, the Texas Tribune reported. “Sustaining the life of the medically fragile child is the paramount concern in this time-sensitive matter,” the ruling said.

The baby was born with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a congenital defect in which one side of the organ is underdeveloped, preventing normal blood flow. The condition can quickly become fatal if it is left untreated.
According to court documents obtained last month by The Associated Press, the newborn was in critical condition and “suffering from potential complications” following heart surgery in Texas.

The parents had turned to surrogacy after efforts involving in vitro fertilization treatments failed. They signed a contract in August 2025 with West — a cardiac nurse who was living in Anchorage, Alaska — that included a clause stipulating the pregnancy could be terminated if there was a “fetal abnormality.”

West said the parents tried to invoke the clause after the heart defect was diagnosed, but she refused to comply. She ultimately headed to Texas, where her case was championed by state Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for a U.S. Senate seat this fall.

With Paxton’s assistance, West got an order directing that the newborn get necessary lifesaving care in Texas after he was born. The parents had planned for him to get that care in their native California.
Judges in Alaska and Texas ultimately deferred to the California ruling, according to West’s Supreme Court filing.
West alleges that Ahmed and Gilkar violated their surrogacy agreement by seeking custody in California. She said the agreement had called for any legal challenges to be heard in Alaska.
West contended that the California decision should be tossed out because she did not get proper due process, and she said she is being kept in the dark about the baby’s health.
In a court filing, West said that “without relief, she will receive no further information about the child she carried for 37 weeks and fought to save.”
The parents’ attorney said that they are focused on the baby’s health and that West is engaged in “political theater.”

title: Postal worker threw out 300 mail-in ballots out of self-described ‘laziness,’ DOJ says
summary: Postal worker threw out 300 mail-in ballots out of self-described ‘laziness,’ DOJ says
story: WASHINGTON — An overwhelmed U.S. postal worker in Utah threw 300 mail-in ballots into a parking lot dumpster shortly before the state’s June 23 primary election in which both Democrats and Republicans were on the ballot, Justice Department officials said Tuesday.

The 34-year-old mail carrier told investigators that he did not have a political agenda and that he tossed other mail when he ditched the ballots, Melissa Holyoak, U.S. attorney for the District of Utah, said. She said roughly 95% of voters do so by mail in the state, and it wasn’t clear yet whether they were able to eventually cast ballots.
According to a government memo, Damon Matai Seei told investigators that he wanted to toss out advertisements to “lighten his workload” after feeling overwhelmed.

“He claims he simply made a ‘poor decision’ out of ‘frustration’ and ‘laziness,’” the memo said. He didn’t intend to toss any ballots, they said. Seei is no longer with the U.S. Postal Service. He pleaded not guilty Tuesday to a charge of destruction and delay of mail.

Justice Department officials held a news conference in Washington to announce the charge as part of its efforts to promote “election integrity.” Federal prosecutors have made possible voter fraud — which is rare — a priority, as President Donald Trump insists without evidence that noncitizens are voting en masse and has sought to limit mail-in ballots. The Supreme Court last week refused to allow the president’s mail-in restrictions to be enforced.

Trump has repeatedly made false claims that he won the 2020 election and has falsely claimed he won the popular vote in 2016, yet the Trump administration has struggled during both terms to bring cases showing evidence of significant voter fraud. That’s despite a massive effort in Trump’s second term to obtain voter registration records from states in an attempt to determine if there were any noncitizens registered.
So far during the president’s second term, the Justice Department has charged 70 voter-fraud-related cases, officials said Tuesday. More than 170 million people are registered to vote in the U.S.
Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said there were more cases in the works, but he didn’t provide further details or a timeline.
“Under the leadership of President Trump and Attorney General Blanche, this department is committed to protecting the vote of American citizens,” he said.

The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, meanwhile, is revving up a long-standing election monitoring program but putting a new emphasis on “ballot security” and staffing the effort with newly hired conservative personnel who have replaced longtime career employees, hundreds of whom have departed en masse since Trump returned to office. The Civil Rights Division’s efforts to seize voter rolls have resulted in a string of court losses — with 25 courts ruling against the federal government.

Voting rights experts say isolated instances of fraud do happen, as do issues with voting machines, but not on a scale that could have changed the outcome of the 2020 presidential election, which was won by Democrat Joe Biden.

But the materials that the Justice Department releases could help feed Trump’s broader narrative about elections. And with the majority of voters disapproving of Trump’s presidency and saying his policies have hurt the economy, Republicans are facing a tough midterms picture.

Earlier this month, the Justice Department rolled out five voting-related cases, four of which were brought against noncitizens. Last week, the Justice Department announced that 16 individuals had been charged in election-related cases, with a news release mentioning that at least 10 of them were lawful permanent residents of the United States. The defendants were originally from Mexico, Nigeria, India, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Antigua and Barbuda, Venezuela, and Colombia.

There was also a defendant from Russia: Victoria Aquilina, a 42-year-old Russian national who entered the United States as an au pair in her early 20s, was charged with casting a ballot in the 2024 election.

Trump — who, until he won the 2024 election, faced federal criminal charges over his efforts to overturn his 2020 loss in the lead-up to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol — said earlier this year that Republicans should “nationalize the voting.”
Democrats, meanwhile, have launched an “unprecedented” effort to combat potential disruption of the 2026 midterm elections.
Seei’s next court date is Nov. 30. His federal public defender did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Simone Biles says three masked men burglarized her home and stole her car
summary: Olympic gold medalist Simone Biles is down one luxury car and up one security dog after three masked men stole her Porsche GTS, she told her TikTok followers on Monday.
story: Olympic gold medalist Simone Biles is down one luxury car and up one security dog after three masked men stole her Porsche GTS, she told her TikTok followers on Monday.
“Get ready with me to pick up my new car,” the gymnast said with an upbeat squeal as she applied makeup in her bathroom.
Biles, 29, said the robbery happened during her last months in Chicago and is partially responsible for why she and her husband, Jonathan Owens, now have a Dobermann Pinscher.
“I feel like I need a reality TV show,” Biles said. “The things that happen to me are absolute insanity.”
Chicago police said it could not provide an incident report to NBC News.
In recent years, several high-profile athletes across multiple sports have reported home break-ins and robberies.

Kansas City Chiefs players Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce were both robbed in October 2024. The homes of basketball pros Sabrina Ionescu of the New York Liberty and Karl-Anthony Towns of the New York Knicks were robbed in 2025. The home of Shedeur Sanders of the Cleveland Browns was robbed by four men as he played a game earlier this year.
Biles said her old car was recovered but she and Owens, a safety for the Indianapolis Colts, decided to get a new one anyway: “When they turned that thing on, I was sold,” she said.
The world’s most decorated gymnast made headlines in June when she revealed on social media that she almost died, though she did not share the circumstances.
“I’m not one to normally share things like this because I value privacy in today’s age,” Biles said in a post, “but almost dying wasn’t on my bingo card earlier this week.”

title: ICE officer who shot man in Austin was issued a body cam but wasn’t wearing it
summary: The officer was issued a body camera but officials said it was not clear why he was not wearing it. Another officer’s body cam only captured partial footage of the shooting.
story: AUSTIN, Texas — The ICE officer who shot a Venezuelan man in Austin on Sunday, leaving a bullet lodged in his back, was issued a body camera but was not wearing it during the shooting, two officials with the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News.

The officials said it was not clear why the officer was not wearing his body camera. Another ICE officer who was in the same vehicle was wearing a body camera, the officials said. That camera captured partial footage of the incident, but the footage does not include the moment of the shooting, the officials said.

Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was shot early Sunday afternoon by an ICE officer while making deliveries as a DoorDash driver. He was taken to a hospital and, four hours after he was shot, was taken into immigration custody at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas, his attorney said. The bullet remains in his back.
On Tuesday, a federal judge granted an emergency order temporarily blocking deportation proceedings against Garcés Pérez, according to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch.

The Travis County District Attorney’s Office also sent a letter to DHS and ICE leadership requesting that Garcés Pérez be allowed to remain in the country since he is “a material witness” in their criminal investigation into the shooting.

Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis shared on Tuesday evening some of the first video footage obtained by the department as part on their probe into the shooting. The videos came from an off-duty officer who captured part of the encounter between ICE and Garcés Pérez, as well as the sound of three gunshots, using his personal dash cam and cellphone.
After this, the off-duty officer alerted his colleagues to the shooting, allowing Austin police to quickly respond to the scene.
Davis said they are seeking the public’s help in obtaining any video evidence that can help them piece together the pursuit that preceded the shooting.

The day after he was shot, Garcés Pérez began “experiencing an inability to move his arm,” attorney Lincoln-Goldfinch said on social media. He was taken to the hospital Monday afternoon for several hours and then sent back to the detention center, she said.
The DHS did not respond to requests for comment about Lincoln-Goldfinch’s statements.
Earlier Monday, Garcés Pérez told a news conference via phone from detention that he was in a lot of pain and wasn’t getting the medical care he needed.

Lincoln-Goldfinch alleged in a social media post that after Garcés Pérez spoke out at the news conference, guards at the detention center “forcibly took the tablet from his hands, revoked his communication privileges, and moved him out of the infirmary into an isolated room with a flat bed that cannot be adjusted like a medical bed.”
He was then taken to the hospital around 5 p.m. after losing his ability to move his arm, she said.
“Wilber reports that he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly during that transfer,” she said in the post.
Lincoln-Goldfinch said Garcés Pérez told her on Tuesday morning that doctors spoke to him about his care and gave him morphine for his pain.

“We now understand that the gunshot fractured his clavicle and that he has significant swelling and is wearing a sling,” she wrote. “We still do not have clarity about the cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced.”
The attorney said Garcés Pérez was discharged from the hospital around midnight and taken back to the detention center, where he is receiving Tylenol and ibuprofen for his ongoing pain.
“He remains in isolation, on a flat bed, and without the tablet he previously used to communicate,” she said.

“We are asking for his communication privileges to be immediately restored and for him to be provided an appropriate medical bed and adequate medical care,” she said. “Most importantly, we are continuing to advocate for Wilber’s IMMEDIATE release.”

Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, said on social media that “despite losing movement on his left side and having a bullet lodged next to his spine, ICE has forced Wilber Rafael out of the hospital and back to the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas.”
He said that he and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, would visit Garcés Pérez on Wednesday, check on his condition and demand his release.
A DHS spokesperson said in a statement late Sunday that Garcés Pérez was in stable condition and was in federal custody pending removal from the U.S.
A senior administration official told NBC News on Monday that Garcés Pérez did not have a criminal history beyond being in the country illegally.

According to Lincoln-Goldfinch, Garcés Pérez entered the country legally and was seeking asylum. She said Garcés Pérez had filed a change of address in immigration court, but received a notice to appear in court at the old address and never got it. Because he missed his immigration hearing, Garcés Pérez was ordered deported in absentia, according to his attorney.

On Monday, Lincoln-Goldfinch shared Garcés Pérez’s account of the shooting, saying he was making a delivery when “an unmarked black truck sideswiped him.” She said he didn’t know it was ICE as the truck chased him as he tried to make a U-turn, and then “pulled him out of the car.”

Previously, DHS has accused immigrants involved in shootings with ICE of using their cars as weapons while fleeing agents, without offering evidence of its claims. But it did not make the accusation in the case of Garcés Pérez or in the case of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was fatally shot in Biddeford, Maine, in July during a traffic stop.

ICE Director David Venturella previously told NBC News that every ICE officer and agent would be equipped with body cameras by the end of August, adding the agency would allow the “expedited release” of bodycam footage “when appropriate.” Further delaying that timeline is the possibility of DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin potentially switching or adding new vendors for body cameras.

A person who witnessed the aftermath of the shooting but who requested anonymity because he is going through immigration proceedings told Noticias Telemundo that he was waiting on customers at the ice cream shop where he works when he heard gunshots and ran outside, where he saw immigration agents surrounding a car.

“I approached the car and saw a man who looked sad and with his eyes full of tears. I asked him what happened to him, and he just told me, ‘I was shot in the back,’” said the person, a Mexican immigrant who has lived in the U.S. for more than two decades.
“You aren’t prepared to see someone like that. It makes you very angry, it pains you and you don’t know what to do,” he said.

A social media video verified by NBC News captures the sound of tires screeching followed by a person exiting a dark-colored SUV as a blue sedan is stopped next to it, both vehicles facing each other. The sedan appears to be damaged on the passenger side.

At least three gunshots are heard as the person approaches the sedan and runs up to it as it slowly lurches forward. The video shows the person standing next to the sedan’s driver’s side as it stops in front of an intersection.

Another video shows the blue sedan with its driver’s side door open and Garcés Pérez hunched over in the driver’s seat, holding his left upper chest, near his shoulder, as multiple law enforcement officers gather around.
The woman taking the video says, “Why did he do that to him?” The officers tell her that an ambulance is coming.

The video shows Garcés Pérez being taken out of the car and handcuffed behind his back. The agents make him sit on the ground. There appears to be a large bloodstain down his back. The officers cut open the back of his shirt, revealing a bullet hole.
An officer asks the woman taking the video if she saw what happened. In Spanish, she replies that “they just shot him because he didn’t want to stop” his vehicle.
“This is unjust,” she says as she’s recording the video.
Julia Ainsley reported from Washington, D.C., Daniella Silva from New York and Albinson Linares from Austin, Texas.

title: Trump administration cuts ACA coverage for 750,000 people it says were ‘fraudulently’ enrolled
summary: The Trump administration is removing hundreds of thousands of enrollees from Obamacare plans, claiming that many were receiving subsidies they didn’t qualify for and that some did not even exist.
story: The Trump administration is removing hundreds of thousands of enrollees from Affordable Care Act plans, claiming that many were receiving subsidies they didn’t qualify for and that some did not even exist. The announcement is the latest effort by the administration to argue that fraud has inflated ACA enrollment, even as experts question the scale of the alleged fraud.

Vice President JD Vance and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz — who have teamed up on a broader push to root out fraud in government health programs — said Tuesday that roughly 750,000 people have had their ACA coverage canceled. The administration did not provide details about who lost coverage or how those individuals were informed.
The cuts, Vance said, would save U.S. taxpayers $2.2 billion.
“These programs are deserving, they are important, but they’re not going to exist unless we stop the fraud,” Vance said at a news conference.

During the Biden administration, ACA enrollment increased from about 11 million to a record 24 million, when pandemic-era enhanced tax credits expanded who was eligible for subsidies. ACA enrollment declined by roughly 3 million people this year after those enhanced subsidies expired, making monthly premiums significantly more expensive for millions of people.

In an interview with NBC News in March, Oz claimed that some of the enrollment increase — around 4 million to 5 million — has been driven by fraud, particularly by insurance brokers, who help people find and sign up for health plans. He said some brokers enrolled people without their knowledge to collect commission fees from insurers.
In other cases, Oz said, people’s incomes made them ineligible for receiving subsidies, they had mistakenly signed up for duplicate plans or they did not exist at all.
“In fact, the fact that we have 23 million makes me think we have too many participants in the ACA,” Oz said at the time. “It’s too high of a number.”
Oz reiterated his claim during the news conference Tuesday, saying, “Obamacare had 10 million enrollees from 2015 to 2020. During Covid, it went up to 22 million people.”
“So the question becomes, what happened?” he said. “Well, the guardrails were weakened, and the prior administration decided not to enforce the weakened guardrails.”
Oz said the administration looked at a combination of factors it considered suspicious.

The people had been enrolled with the help of a broker or agent, had never filed a claim, had their entire monthly premium covered by federal tax credits, and either had no Social Security number or immigration documents that the CMS could verify in real time.

“We call them phantoms, because we believe most of them don’t exist or they had no idea they had coverage,” he said. “We believe that because we’ve been writing them, telexing them, FedExing, whatever we possibly can do to get in touch with them. They won’t answer.”
It’s unclear whether the enrollees who lost their coverage were paying their premiums.

Health policy experts say fraud exists in the ACA, as well as the entire U.S. healthcare system. In 2025, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that 2.3 million people were improperly receiving enhanced tax credits.
Experts, however, question how widespread the fraud in the program is — and whether the administration is overstating its role in the ACA’s enrollment increases.
Much of the enrollment decline, experts say, isn’t due to eliminating fraud but because coverage became unaffordable after the end of the enhanced tax credits.

“It is entirely possible that many of these people were enrolled without their knowledge or were so-called phantom enrollees,” said Cynthia Cox, director of the program on the ACA at KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group. “It is also entirely possible that many of these people were legitimately enrolled and simply did not respond in time.”
Vance said that the administration is also investigating an additional 419,000 people it says may be improperly enrolled.
“They had something about their story that was a little bit different than what we expected from the 100% fraud story,” Oz said at the news conference. “We’re giving them another chance.”

title: GOP senator calls for subpoenaing Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden over their business dealings
summary: A Republican senator is calling for an investigation into the business dealings of Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden following the revelation that a Russian oligarch paid for Trump Jr.’s post-wedding festivities in the Caribbean earlier this year.
story: A Republican senator is calling for an investigation into the business dealings of Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden following the revelation that a Russian oligarch paid for Trump Jr.’s post-wedding festivities in the Caribbean earlier this year.

Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, sent a letter Monday to the leaders of the Senate Judiciary Committee, Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, and ranking member Dick Durbin, D-Ill., requesting that the panel subpoena the president’s eldest son as well as former President Joe Biden’s son for testimony.

Curtis wants the two to provide information about “their past business dealings, relationships with foreign individuals and entities, gifts or other benefits they have received, and any instances in which their relationship to the President was invoked or understood to provide value.”

Curtis noted that Hunter Biden has “denied involving his father in his business dealings,” but the senator suggested he benefited from his father’s service in public office. He also expressed concern about Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev, who has ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin, paying for Trump Jr.’s post-wedding celebration in May.

“These reports raise legitimate questions about foreign access to members of a sitting president’s family and whether such relationships can create actual or perceived expectations of favorable treatment,” Curtis said. “They also may create expectations of a returned favor that would not be in the best interests of the American people or our allies, and could even create national security vulnerabilities.”

In a post on X Tuesday, Curtis criticized the president’s son. “A toaster is a wedding gift. A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else. Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden’s foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now. ‘Trust us’ was not enough then, and it is not enough now.”
A Judiciary Committee spokesperson said that the panel received Curtis’ letter and that hearing dates for the committee are extremely limited through the end of the year.
Asked about the letter on Tuesday afternoon, Grassley declined to comment, saying that he hadn’t read it yet.
Durbin, however, voiced support for Curtis’ request.

“For the Committee to ignore this matter is to run the risk of being complicit in a coverup,” he said, noting that Hunter Biden had given a sworn deposition to Congress about allegations against him, while Trump Jr. has not.

Republicans have for years accused Hunter Biden of using his family’s connections to enrich himself through business deals in Ukraine and China, and several House committees investigated the allegations.
The Trump Organization, where Trump Jr. serves as executive vice president, and Hunter Biden didn’t respond to requests for comment. NBC News also reached out to the White House.

In a post on X, Hunter Biden responded to Curtis’ request for his testimony: “I say bring it on. I’ve already given more than seven hours of sworn testimony. More than three dozen witnesses testified across two chambers. I had no foreign business dealings while my father was president. None. I painted paintings, and I still do. I’ll sit next to Don Jr. and testify any time, any place. Eric and Jared can join us too. No need for a subpoena. Let’s all do it tomorrow.”
Donald Trump Jr. and his wife Bettina Trump acknowledged Kremlev paid for their post-wedding celebration on a pair of Caribbean islands after ProPublica reported the connection.
In a joint Instagram post, they referred to the paid-for celebration as “an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful.”
They also said in the post that the vacation had been planned separately from their wedding, but when their nuptial plans changed, “we simply decided to get married before it.”

Last week, the president defended his son’s decision to accept the cash gift from Kremlev, but claimed that he has paid him back. “It’s totally allowed. But as I understand it, he paid him back. He didn’t want to have that, so I hear he paid him back.”

Some Republicans, especially in tight re-election races, are distancing themselves from Trump. Curtis, however, is currently serving his first term in the Senate and is not up for re-election until 2030.

title: Lionel Richie undergoes heart procedure, will ‘take some time off’
summary: Lionel Richie underwent a heart procedure leading to the postponement of at least three shows and casting doubt on an upcoming Las Vegas residency, a representative for the famed singer and producer said Tuesday.
story: Lionel Richie underwent a heart procedure leading to the postponement of at least three shows and casting doubt on an upcoming Las Vegas residency, a representative for the famed singer and producer said Tuesday.

Richie was scheduled to perform with Earth, Wind & Fire at the Chase Center in San Francisco on Saturday night, at the United Center in Chicago on Sept, 30 and at the Schottenstein Center in Columbus, Ohio on Oct. 2.
All three shows have been postponed with no makeup date immediately set, according to box office employees in San Francisco and Columbus and a statement by the United Center in Chicago.
“Lionel underwent a common procedure for Atrial fibrillation (AFib),” a representative for Richie said in a statement.
“The doctor said everything went perfectly. Lionel is doing great but will take some time off and will be back on stage soon.”
Richie has a residency scheduled at the Encore Theater at Wynn Las Vegas, with shows set for Oct. 14, 16, 17 and Nov. 11, 13 and 14.
A representative for the Las Vegas hotel and casino could not be immediately reached for comment on Tuesday.
Richie has experienced troubling medical incidents in recent months.
He was playing in St. Paul, Minnesota, on June 24 when he was forced to end the show early, telling fans he was feeling dizzy.
He was performing “Dancing on the Ceiling” when he sat down on stage, stood up and walked a few feet before sitting down again.
He also reportedly checked into a St. Louis hospital after feeling weak and dehydrated following an Aug. 29 show.

title: Nolan Wells’ family vows to ‘never stop’ seeking the truth after grand jury report
summary: Nolan Wells’ parents and their attorneys called on Mississippi to continue pursuing a fuller picture of the “truth” in the teenager’s death at a press conference Tuesday.
story: Nolan Wells’ parents and their attorneys called on Mississippi to continue pursuing a fuller picture of the “truth” in the teenager’s death at a press conference Tuesday.
The press conference was held a day after the Jackson County district attorney said a state grand jury will not pursue charges in the teenager’s July Fourth death.

“Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McArthur will have you accept that Nolan Wells’ death can be summarized in three words: ‘We’ll never know,’” attorney Ben Crump said. “But Nolan’s family offers three other words: ‘We’ll never stop.’”
Crump, in his remarks, insinuated that the district attorney’s investigation was not exhaustive and should continue until the cause of Wells’ death is made clear.
Attorney Ben Crump and Nolan Wells' parents speak out
Wells’ mother, Christine Wells-Wonsley, said she received a text message from the district attorney at 7:54 p.m. Monday, and that the report was released shortly after.
“To me, that action shows a lack of empathy,” she said.
Wells-Wonsley continued: “What we have learned is that we still have no answers, and the report reinforced the fact that Nolan was not given a thorough, transparent and honest investigation.”

Wells, 18, was last seen celebrating the July 4 holiday with friends on Horn Island, a barrier reef off Mississippi accessible only by boat. The friends he was with that day have said they had to leave the island early because their boat was taking on water, and that Wells opted to stay behind for the rest of the day. His mother has said he never returned home, even though his friends said that he told them he planned to catch a ride back to the mainland with others.
His body was found at the northwestern tip of the island July 6, Crump has said.

In the aftermath of Wells’ death, Crump pointed the blame toward the friends Wells was with on that day, all of whom are white, and alleged that race was involved. Wells appeared to be one of the few Black people on the island that day, according to photos and videos shared of the celebrations.
District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath attempted to put that idea to rest with Tuesday’s statement.

In a video message, she said the grand jury returned a “no true bill,” meaning it did not find sufficient evidence to indict anyone with a crime. A partially redacted copy of the grand jury report was also posted to the DA’s Facebook page.

“There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan’s disappearance and death were racially motivated,” Myers McIlrath said. “Nolan’s friends loved Nolan, and Nolan loved them. Nolan chose to stay on the island that day, and there is not a scintilla of evidence to contradict that.”
She also took aim at Crump and his team in the statement, saying they also previously informed her office that they’d found no evidence a crime had been committed against Wells.
Crump, in turn, said in a statement: “This grand jury result leaves us with more questions than answers. Nolan’s family will not rest until we know what happened to him, and neither will we.”

The Rev. Al Sharpton, who has been an advocate for the family, said skepticism is warranted from Wells’ parents and those following the case. “Mississippi’s history painfully teaches us exactly why families should never be expected to simply accept unanswered questions surrounding the death of a young Black person,” the civil rights advocate said in a statement Tuesday.
Crump, along with Wells’ parents, commissioned an independent autopsy, which found the cause of the teenager’s death was “undetermined.” It did, however, find two bruises on the back of Wells’ head.

“To this day, not one person has explained how they got there,” Crump added in the statement. “We don’t know how Nolan died, and neither does the state of Mississippi. Mississippi must keep investigating.”
Crump and Wells-Wonsley both spoke about the apparent blunt force trauma again Tuesday at the news conference and called for answers.
Crump called on the district attorney to release the full autopsy report from the medical examiner’s office.

Coroner Bruce Lynd will not be releasing the state’s autopsy report, telling NBC News “the autopsy report, which may include a toxicology report, cannot be released because the release of autopsy reports” is limited by Mississippi law.

The grand jury, which investigated the case, concluded that there was no evidence that Wells had any sort of physical altercation or argument with anyone the day he was last seen. It added “that the position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr. Wells’ body is consistent with drowning.”

Crump and Wells’ parents have previously rejected the theory that he simply drowned, citing the teenager’s athleticism and ability to swim. Those who know the area well, though, told NBC News it is not uncommon for even a good swimmer to be swept away by the currents.

The state’s chief medical examiner and a forensic pathologist retained by Wells’ family both “opined that the cause and manner of Mr. Wells’ death is undetermined and that drowning is a diagnosis of exclusion,” according to the grand jury report. It noted, however, that neither has ruled out accidental drowning as a cause.

Crump said there will be another press conference in Orlando, Florida, later this week to discuss the investigation into Wells’ cellphone. The friends on the boat had his phone and brought it back to the mainland from Horn Island on July 4. They said Wells accidentally left it with them, but his parents have refuted that assertion, asking what teenager would leave their phone behind?

title: The best editor-approved planners and agendas for even the busiest schedules
summary: I rounded up some of the best planners and agendas to help you get organized this year, complete with calendars, to-do lists and more.
story: Things like smart clocks, digital calendars and to-do lists help you stay organized and on top of your routine. Traditional planners also keep your schedule on track and typically don’t come at a high price either. Finding the best planner for your personal routine, however, involves more than simply picking up the first one you see.

Depending on your routine, the best planner or agenda for you will likely have more than just blank paper — it should come with features like calendars, tabs, sections for to-do lists, lists of important dates and holidays, and at the least, lined pages. Plus, a great planner should be able to keep up with your lifestyle, which means it has to have a durable cover to help keep it together for months.

To find the best planners and agendas for this year, I gathered recommendations from my colleagues and included options from brands I’ve used myself. Read more about our favorite analog planners below.

This hardcover planner is available as a mid-year planner and as an academic year option. It’s available in several styles and it includes calendars and weekly planning sections for each month. It also has a section for dates, reminders, contact information and more. Each calendar also has a section on the side for important notes.

In addition to the weekly planning sections and calendars and daily to-do lists, the back of the planner also has dotted and lined pages for additional note taking. It also has a ribbon to place between pages to help keep your place. The planner, which has 192 pages, is available as a hardcover or as a softer spiral-bound option.

Since it’s a full-size planner (read: large), it is better for keeping in one place, like your office desk, rather than trekking back and forth daily, according to Evans. Also, while it isn’t dated, it’s a daily planner, so it’s best if used for day-of obligations as opposed to for planning weeks or months in advance.

Available in 20 colors, this planner from Amazon comes with a ribbon bookmark, an elastic band and 160 lined pages. It is also available in blank, dotted and 252-page options and you can also get it in multipacks.

While it doesn’t have calendars and pre-made to-do lists, it’s far from plain, but great for people who want a simple planner that also doesn’t cost a ton of money. It has a pocket on the inside and it comes with multiple lined adhesive labels, which you can use to write your name, contact information and other important details in case you lose it. title: Princess Diana Expressed Doubts About Her Wedding. This Family Member Stopped Her From Calling It Off
summary: Princess Diana expressed doubts over her wedding but was stopped by this close family member, her brother Charles Spencer writes in his memoir.
story: Before her famous royal wedding to the now King Charles III, Princess Diana expressed serious doubts about going through with the marriage, according to her brother.

In his new memoir “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” Diana’s younger brother, Charles Spencer, recalls learning that the princess had gone to their father, John Spencer, expressing that “she could not go through with marriage to a man who clearly did not love her.”
Diana and Charles were first linked in July 1980 and became engaged in February 1981.

Spencer details that Diana had attended the birthday party of Prince Andrew with her fiancé, whom she was very excited to be reunited with, as he had just returned that day from an official trip to New York. Andrew has since been stripped of his royal titles.

Spencer goes on to write, “Diana had dreamt of spending the party at Windsor Castle at her fiancé’s side. But he had shown next to no interest in her, and she — deeply hurt, confused and increasingly concerned — danced with others, including me, instead.”
Diana went to her father to share her feelings of uncertainty after that night. However, Charles Spencer says he didn’t find out the details of the conversation until much later.

Diana’s father, John Spencer, did not support her idea of ending the engagement. “My father was appalled and said it was impossible to pull out of such an enormous commitment at that point,” Spencer writes.
Spencer reflects on why he believes their father responded that way, pointing to his long connection to the royal family and sense of duty to the monarchy.
“He always adored Diana, but what she was proposing was counter to the code on which he had been brought up, and which he never seemed to question.”
Ending the engagement, Spencer says, would have meant “deeply embarrassing the Royal Family.”

Diana ultimately went through with the wedding, marrying Charles on July 29, 1981, at St. Paul’s Cathedral in London. Diana called the wedding “the worst day of my life,” in a series of recordings taped in 1991 for a biography titled, “Diana: Her True Story.”
Their marriage would eventually crumble, the royal pair separating in 1992 and finalizing their divorce in 1996, just a year before her death at 36.
Spencer’s account also notes a happier relationship that formed the night of Andrew’s birthday, when Elton John performed.
“The day after Prince Andrew’s party, with her usual impeccable manners, Diana wrote by hand to Elton John, her letter applauding him for his brilliance the previous night” he says.

Spencer says the exchange marked the beginning of a friendship that would continue throughout Diana’s life and ultimately became one of the most memorable moments at Diana’s funeral in 1997, when John performed a reworked version of “Candle in the Wind.”

title: Simone Biles Says Her Porsche Was Stolen After 3 Masked Intruders Broke Into Her Home: ‘Absolute Insanity’
summary: Simone Biles said three masked intruders stole her Porsche during a frightening break-in at a home she shared in Chicago with husband Jonathan Owens.
story: Simone Biles said three masked intruders stole her Porsche during a frightening break-in at a home she shared in Chicago with husband Jonathan Owens.
The legendary gymnast described what happened in a TikTok video on Sept. 21 in which she wrote in the caption that the luxury car has since been recovered.
Biles, 29, said in the video that she was getting ready to pick up her new car.

“Feel like I need a new car because during our last few months in Chicago, three men in masks came to our house and stole my Porsche,” she said. “Stole the GTS. But that’s another story. If you guys want to know, I’ll do a story time on that.”
Owens, 31, who is a safety for the Indianapolis Colts, previously played in Chicago for the Bears in 2024 and 2025. It’s not clear when the alleged burglary occurred.
“I feel like I need a reality TV show,” Biles said. “The things that happen to me are absolute insanity, and so it would be really easy for producers to just film regularly.”

Several high-profile athletes have been the victims of theft in recent years. A Seattle man was charged in 2025 for allegedly burglarizing the homes of multiple Seattle Mariners players as well as former Seattle Seahawks star Richard Sherman and Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Blake Snell.
In 2024, the homes of Kansas City Chiefs stars Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce and Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow were burglarized.
Biles added that she and Owens have brought in additional protection after the car theft.
“That is one of the reasons why we also got our Doberman,” she said.

The revelation by the seven-time Olympic gold medalist came three months after she had a health scare she called “one of, if not the scariest experience of my life.” Biles shared the unspecified medical issue on her Instagram story on June 6.

“I’m not one to normally share things like this because I value privacy in today’s age,” Biles captioned a photo of her wrist with hospital bands on it. “But almost dying wasn’t on my bingo card earlier this week.”
Owens was in training camp with the Colts at the time.
“This was one of, if not the scariest experience of my life. Especially since Jonathan was in Indy for practices,” she wrote.
She then shared on her Instagram story on July 23 that she had a “procedure” that required a hospital visit.
Biles did specify what the procedure concerned or if it was connected to her health scare in June.
